content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulties in social communication, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors. The clinical progression of children diagnosed with ASD can vary significantly, and some research suggests that certain children may no longer meet the diagnostic criteria for ASD over time. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the proportion of preschool-aged children (diagnosed with ASD before the age of six) who continued to meet the diagnostic criteria for ASD at follow-up, which ranged from one year to as long as 19 years later. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, was conducted up to July 2021. Reference lists of relevant systematic reviews were also examined. Studies included in the review were required to follow participants for at least one year, use consistent diagnostic measures at both baseline and follow-up, and include at least 10 participants. All participants were under six years old at the time of their initial diagnosis and were followed up before the age of 19. Data were extracted on study characteristics, the proportion of children meeting ASD diagnostic criteria at baseline and follow-up, and changes in scores on measures assessing ASD dimensions (social communication, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors). Risk of bias was assessed using a modified version of the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. Depending on the data available, either a random-effects meta-analysis or a narrative synthesis was conducted. Prognostic factor analyses were also performed to identify variables that might predict diagnostic outcomes. A total of 49 studies met the inclusion criteria, and data were extracted from 42 of these studies, encompassing 11,740 participants. Most studies (60%) were conducted in North America, with 31% in Europe and the UK, and 10% in Asia. Over half of the studies (52%) were published before 2014. The mean age of participants at baseline was 3.19 years, with a range of 1.13 to 5.0 years, and the mean age at follow-up was 6.12 years, ranging from 3.0 to 12.14 years. The average follow-up duration was 2.86 years, with a range of 1.0 to 12.41 years. The majority of participants were boys (81%), and over half of the studies (60%) primarily included children with intellectual disabilities (IQ < 70). The mean sample size across studies was 272, with a range of 10 to 8,564 participants. Most studies (69%) used a single diagnostic assessment tool, while 24% used two tools, and 7% used three or more tools. In 41% of studies, diagnoses were determined by a multidisciplinary team. However, no data were available on changes in social communication or restricted and repetitive behaviors and interests between baseline and follow-up. Of the 42 studies with available data, 34 studies (69% of all included studies, n = 11,129 participants) were included in a meta-analysis. The results indicated that 92% of participants (95% confidence interval: 89% to 95%) continued to meet the diagnostic criteria for ASD from baseline to follow-up. However, the quality of the evidence was rated as low due to study limitations and inconsistencies. Most studies (95%) were judged to have a high risk of bias. Additionally, none of the included studies provided separate domain scores for social communication or restricted and repetitive behaviors at both baseline and follow-up, preventing an analysis of changes in these specific areas. Conflict of interest details were reported in 24 studies, while funding support was disclosed in 30 studies. Twelve studies did not provide information on funding sources, and two studies reported no funding support. Declared funding sources included government, university, non-governmental organizations, or charity groups. It was deemed unlikely that funding sources significantly influenced the outcomes, given the nature of prognosis studies. In conclusion, approximately nine out of ten children diagnosed with ASD before the age of six continued to meet the diagnostic criteria for ASD at follow-up one or more years later. However, the evidence was uncertain due to heterogeneity, high risk of bias, and the limited number of studies using contemporary diagnostic systems such as DSM-5 or ICD-11. Future research should focus on well-designed, prospective studies that assess the prognosis of ASD diagnoses using modern diagnostic methods across diverse populations. These studies should also investigate a range of relevant prognostic factors.
